I have considered the submissions from both the sides alongwith record.
8. At first, this court will decide the maintainability of present revision petition against the impugned order.
As per section 397(2) Cr.P.C., the power of revision shall not be exercised in relation to any interlocutory order.

Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Amar Nath vs. State of Haryana, AIR 1977 SC 2185 has observed as under:-
"The main question which falls for determination in this appeal is as to, the what is the connotation of the term "interlocutory order" as appearing in sub-s. (2) of s. 397 which bars any revision of such an order by the High Court.

entities.text: Amar Nath vs. State of Haryana, AIR 1977 SC 2185
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The term "interlocutory order" is a term of well-known legal significance and does not present any serious diffident.

It has been used in various statutes including the Codeof Civil Procedure,
Letters Patent of the High Courts and other like statutes.
In Webster's New World Dictionary "interlocutory" has been defined as an order other than final decision.
Decided cases have laid down that interlocutory orders to be appealable must be those which decide 'the rights and liabilities of the parties concerning a particular aspect.
It seems to, us that the term "interlocutory order" in s. 397(2) of the 1973 Code has been used in a restricted sense and not in any broad or artistic sense.
It merely denotes orders of a purely interim or temporary nature which do not decide or touch the important rights, or the liabilities of the parties.

Any order which substantially affects the, right of the accused, or decides certain rights of the parties cannot be said to be an interlocutory order so as to bar a revision to the High Court against that order, because that would be against the very object which formed the basis for insertion of this particular provision in s. 397 of the, 1973 Code.

Thus, for Digitally signed by SUNIL SUNIL GUPTA Date:
GUPTA 2024.02.15 18:10:50 +0530 instance, orders summoning witnesses,
adjourning cases, passing orders for bail, calling for reports and such other steps in Sukrat Bajaj vs Vinod Kumar And Ors on 15 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/53455884/
4 aid of the pending proceeding, may no doubt amount to interlocutory orders against which no revision would lie under s. 397 (2) of the 1973 Code.

sentences.text: But orders which are matters of moment and which affect or adjudicate the rights of the accused or a particular aspect of the trial cannot be said to be interlocutory order so as to be.
outside the purview of the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court."

9. This aspect was further clarified by a three judge bench of Hon'ble Apex Court in Madhu Limaye Vs. The State of Maharashtra, AIR 1978 SC 47 wherein it was held that an interpretation and universal application of the principle that what is not a final order must be an interlocutory order is neither warranted nor justified.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Hon'ble Court was of the view that a judgment or order may be final for one purpose and interlocutory for another and it was held that it was neither advisable nor possible to make a catalog of orders to demonstrate which kind of orders would be purely interlocutory and which kind of orders would be final and then to prepare an exhaustive list of those types of orders which will fall between the too.

10. This Court is also guided by the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in Kamlesh Kumar Vs. State of Jharkhand, AIR 2013 SCW 5952 wherein after relying upon the Constitution Bench judgment in Pranab Kumar Mitra Vs. State of West Bengal 1959 (1) Suppl. SCR 63, it was held as under:-
"28.

sentences.text: While the revisional power of a superior court actually enables it to correct a grave error, the existence of that power does not confer any SUNIL by SUNIL GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.02.15 18:11:01 +0530 corresponding right on a litigant.
This is the reason why, in a given case, a superior court may decline to exercise its power of revision, if the facts and circumstances of the case do not warrant the exercise of its discretion.
This is also the reason why it is felicitously stated that a revision is not a right but only a "procedural facility" available to a party.
If the matter is looked at in this light, the transfer of a case from a Magistrate to a Special Judge does not take away this procedural facility available to the petitioners.

It only changes the forum and as already held above, the petitioners have no right to choose the forum in which to file an appeal or move a petition for revising an interlocutory order."

While Ld. Counsel for revisionist has submitted that the revision petition was maintainable, Ld. Counsel for respondents has submitted that same was not maintainable.
Both the parties have relied upon several judgments in support of their submissions.
Admittedly, none of the judgments relied upon by them has dealt with the specific question before this Court.

Final order or an interlocutory order depending upon the situation whether the said order finally determined the rights of the parties in respect to given stage or was simply a step in and in the course of proceedings like summoning of witnesses,
issuing of commission or order of production of documents etc.

(13) Judged on this criterion, I am of the considered view that an order rejecting bail may be Interlocutory because subsequent applications are maintainable on fresh grounds being shown, or at different stages of enquiry or trial but as against that, the order of grant of ball finally disposes of the application, and the Department's rights are substantially affected in the sense that in a given case it may be possible to show to the Court that there was reasonable apprehension that the presence of the accused is not possible to be secured and that its rights to have the accused face the trial would by vitally affected,
Such an order has to be treated as a final order, in the sense that revision petition against such an order would not be barred.
To hold otherwise would be tantamount to making a magistrate the sow repository of the power to refuse or grant bail.

Such a proposition can certainly be not countenanced,"

Accordingly, it is held that present revision petition is maintainable.

In any case,
Ld. Counsel for revisionist has also invoked Section 439(2) Cr.P.C. so present petition is maintainable.

Reliance is placed on the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in Dolat Ram Vs State of Haryana 1995 SCC (1) 349, wherein the issue before Hon'ble Apex Court was as to whether the order of Hon'ble Punjab & Haryana High Court directing cancellation of anticipatory bail granted to the appellants by Ld. sentences.text: Rejection of bail in a non-bailable case at the initial stage and the cancellation of bail so granted, have to be considered and dealt with on different basis.
Very cogent and overwhelming circumstances are necessary for an order directing the cancellation of the bail, already granted.

Generally speaking, the grounds for cancellation of bail, broadly (illustrative and not exhaustive) are:
interference or attempt to interfere with the due course of administration of Justice or evasion or attempt to evade the due course of justice or abuse of the concession granted to the accused in any manner.
The satisfaction of the court, on the basis of material placed on the record of the possibility of the accused absconding is yet another reason justifying the cancellation of bail.

However, bail once granted should not be cancelled in a mechanical manner without considering whether any supervening circumstances have rendered it no longer conducive to a fair trial to allow the accused to retain his freedom by enjoying the concession of bail during the trial.
These principles, it appears, were lost sight of by the High Court when it decided to cancel the bail, already granted.
The High Court it appears to us overlooked the distinction of the factors relevant for rejecting bail in a nonbailable case in the first instance and the cancellation of bail already granted."

16. Applying the said principles to the case at hand, this Court is of the view that after release of respondent no.1 on bail vide order dated 25.10.2016, his conduct in having collusion with Mr.
J.P.Singh, Counsel for revisionist at that time for ensuring bail for his son/respondent no.2 was clearly an interference with due course of administration of justice.

17. As far as, the prayer for cancellation of bail granted to respondent no.2 vide order dated 14.10.2017 is concerned, it is to be noted that his case is different from the case of his father/respondent no.1.

Although, the genesis of present revision petition lies in the order dated 14.10.2017 of Ld. Magistrate whereby respondent no.2 was admitted to bail however, it is not even the case of revisionist that he had done any overt act to secure bail from Ld. Trial Court.

Though, the allegations of the revisionist are that respondent no.2 was in conspiracy with his father in paying cash to Mr. J.P.
Singh (Advocate), however the very basis of these allegations i.e., proceedings pertaining to CT Case No.2662/2018 does not show anything to that effect.

In the absence of any material to show the complicity of respondent no.2 in interference with administration of justice, this Court is of the view that the impugned order cannot be faulted with as far as same pertains to respondent no.2.
It was the duty of revisionist to place on record enough material which could have pointed out the specific role of respondent no.2 in the entire conspiracy.
Accordingly, the revision petition stands dismissed qua him.

18. Before parting with this order, it is to be noted that both the Ld. Counsels representing opposite sides were on the same page on the point that Bar Council of Delhi was the appropriate authority to rule upon the alleged professional misconduct of Mr. J.P. Singh, Advocate regarding which a complaint has already been made by the revisionist way back in the year 2017.

In that complaint, it was alleged that Mr.
Singh was not returning some blank signed documents of the revisionist.
The documents pertaining to his collusion with respondent no.1 were also filed in the said complaint subsequently in the year 2019.

It has been informed by Ld. Counsel for revisionist that on the failure of Bar Council of Delhi to dispose of the complaint within prescribed period, same has been transferred to Bar Council of India.
Without commenting much on this aspect, it is expected that said complaint would be disposed of expeditiously so that the faith of common man in this noble profession remains unshaken.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
As per section 397(2) Cr.P.C., the power of revision shall not be exercised in relation to any interlocutory order.
Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Amar Nath vs. State of Haryana, AIR 1977 SC 2185 has observed as under:-
"The main question which falls for determination in this appeal is as to, the what is the connotation of the term "interlocutory order" as appearing in sub-s. (2) of s. 397 which bars any revision of such an order by the High Court.
10. This Court is also guided by the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in Kamlesh Kumar Vs. State of Jharkhand, AIR 2013 SCW 5952 wherein after relying upon the Constitution Bench judgment in Pranab Kumar Mitra Vs. State of West Bengal 1959 (1) Suppl. SCR 63, it was held as under:-
"28.
Such an order has to be treated as a final order, in the sense that revision petition against such an order would not be barred.
It is settled law that very cogent and overwhelming circumstances are necessary for an order directing the cancellation of the bail, already granted.
Generally speaking,
the grounds for cancellation of bail, broadly are : interference or attempt to interfere with the due course of administration of justice or evasion or attempt to evade the due course of justice or abuse of the concession granted to the accused in any manner.
The satisfaction of the court on the basis of material placed on the record of the possibility of the accused absconding is yet another reason justifying the cancellation of bail.
However bail once granted should not be cancelled in a mechanical manner without considering whether any supervening circumstances Sukrat Bajaj vs Vinod Kumar And Ors on 15 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/53455884/
6
have rendered it no longer, conductive to a fair trial to allow the accused to retain his freedom by enjoying the concession of bail during the trial.
15. It is settled law that overwhelming circumstances are required to be shown for cancellation of a bail.
16. Applying the said principles to the case at hand, this Court is of the view that after release of respondent no.1 on bail vide order dated 25.10.2016, his conduct in having collusion with Mr.
J.P.Singh, Counsel for revisionist at that time for ensuring bail for his son/respondent no.2 was clearly an interference with due course of administration of justice.
There is inherent condition in a bail order passed in favour of any accused in a criminal case that he shall not interfere with the administration of justice in any manner whatsoever.
He is expected to defend himself as per law but such an expectation will not cover the eventuality of him conniving with the counsel of opposite party by paying him money so that he can help Sukrat Bajaj vs Vinod Kumar And Ors on 15 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/53455884/
8 him/co-accused.
Respondent no.1 by his conduct has shown that he can do anything to get the relief from Court for himself or for his son.
In these circumstances, to maintain the purity of administration of justice and considering the fact that matter is still at the stage of arguments on charge so there is every possibility of him influencing the witnesses in similar manner, this Court is of the view that he does not deserve the liberty of bail granted vide order dated 25.10.2016 of Ld. Magistrate.
Although, the genesis of present revision petition lies in the order dated 14.10.2017 of Ld. Magistrate whereby respondent no.2 was admitted to bail however, it is not even the case of revisionist that he had done any overt act to secure bail from Ld. Trial Court.
Though, the allegations of the revisionist are that respondent no.2 was in conspiracy with his father in paying cash to Mr. J.P.
Singh (Advocate), however the very basis of these allegations i.e., proceedings pertaining to CT Case No.2662/2018 does not show anything to that effect.
In the absence of any material to show the complicity of respondent no.2 in interference with administration of justice, this Court is of the view that the impugned order cannot be faulted with as far as same pertains to respondent no.2.
It was the duty of revisionist to place on record enough material which could have pointed out the specific role of respondent no.2 in the entire conspiracy.
Accordingly, the revision petition stands dismissed qua him.
